reason: A young Greater Spotted Eagle: uniformly blackish-brown with rows of large white drops on the scapulars, median and greater coverts and no buff nape patch; a young Lesser is paler brown with a buff nape and one row of small spots. Meyer's naevia covered both, and Dresser cites the plate under both clanga and pomarina, so the figure decides.

reason: Gould's Falco lanarius (Pallas's and Temminck's sense) is the Saker: he lists this plate under Falco sacer in his own synonymy (Birds of Asia I.5), as do Dresser and Sharpe. The figures agree: brown back with no grey, pale streaked crown, thin moustache, tail spotted not barred.

reason: Falco concolor Temm. is the Sooty Falcon, and the figure is one: uniform pale lead-grey with blackish primaries and no moustache, where a dark Eleonora's Falcon is sooty brown-black. Gould gives the Nile and Abyssinia; Sharpe cites the plate under F. concolor.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM i; the plate

reason: Pale Thrush, not Eyebrowed: the figures have no supercilium, and Gould gives white tips to the two outer tail feathers and Japanese specimens from Temminck. Seebohm (Cat. Birds BM v) cites the plate under Merula pallida.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM v; the plate

reason: Temminck's stapazina is the black-throated morph of the western bird; Dresser cites the plate under his S. rufa (western black-throated). The male's black bib is small and well clear of the wings and the forehead is pale, not the large bib and black-fronted mask of the eastern melanoleuca. Gould's range (S Italy, Dalmatia, Greece) is Temminck's, not the specimens'.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. ii; the plate

reason: Temminck's aurita is the pale-throated morph; both males show a narrow mask from the lores below the eye with the forehead pale, not the black band across the forehead of the eastern melanoleuca (Dresser's Smyrna male). Gould gives N Italy, Sardinia and Naples. Western Black-eared Wheatear.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. ii; the plate

reason: Sylvia leucopogon Meyer is a synonym of nominate cantillans (type locality Sicily; Zuccon et al. 2020). Gould's specimens came from Savi of Pisa and from Temminck, and the male's brick-red throat to flanks with a white belly is not Moltoni's pale pink. Eastern Subalpine Warbler, unless Temminck's birds were Provençal (Western).
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. ii; Zuccon et al. 2020; the plate

reason: Willow Warbler in yellow first-autumn dress, or a yellow Chiffchaff? It is a Phylloscopus, not a Hippolais: slender bill, long yellow supercilium. Pale legs and the long brow say Willow Warbler. Temminck's figures of a wing as short as the Chiffchaff's point the other way. Primary projection and leg colour on Temminck's specimen would decide. The plate is in the copy: leaf 344, engraved 'Yellow Willow Wren. Sylvia Icterina (Vieill.)', pencilled 133.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption on leaf 344 (BHL scan); Gould's text; the plate

reason: Gould's text and figure are the British Rock Pipit: a coastal, resident, dusky olive bird with heavy dark blotches below, on a shore rock. He notes that the continental birds' vinous breast (the Water Pipit) is missing in British examples. Dresser cites the plate under Anthus obscurus. Bechstein's aquaticus is the Water Pipit's name.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. iii; the plate

reason: Gould's neglecta is the Blue-headed Wagtail, nominate M. f. flava, not the Grey-headed thunbergi: the male has a blue-grey head with a bold white supercilium and a white line below the ear-coverts, as Gould describes from continental and Paris birds. Western Yellow Wagtail.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Gould, B. Gt. Brit. III.4 synonymy; the plate

reason: The figures are Chestnut-eared Buntings: chestnut ear-coverts, a grey streaked crown and a streaked black necklace on a white throat. Gould had his birds from China, and Temminck from Japan. Sharpe (Cat. Birds BM xii) puts the plate and Gmelin's lesbia in E. fucata.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xii; the plate

reason: Linaria canescens Gould is the Mealy Redpoll, nominate flammea (Sharpe's Acanthis linaria; Gould's own synonymy in Birds of Great Britain III.51). The figure has a streaked whitish rump and flanks, not a Hoary's. eBird 2025 lumps the redpolls.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xii; Gould, B. Gt. Brit. III.51; the plate

reason: Tetrao hybridus is the Rackelhahn, a hybrid Western Capercaillie x Black Grouse, as Gould himself says. No single species to name.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxii; the plate

reason: Willow Ptarmigan (Ogilvie-Grant puts Temminck's unique brachydactylus there) or a female Rock Ptarmigan? The white winter bird has no black lores, which fits both, and shows only the tip of a small bill. Temminck's specimen, from N Russia via Feldegg, would decide: a deep, broad bill means Willow, a slim one Rock.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxii; the plate

reason: Gould's Otis houbara is the African bird: he separates it from Gray's macqueeni, gives N Africa (and Spain), and the figure has rich tawny upperparts. Dresser and Ogilvie-Grant cite the plate under undulata. African Houbara.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. vii; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxiii; the plate

reason: Sharpe (Cat. Birds BM xxiv) makes this plate the basis of Ochthodromus pyrrhothorax, the black-fronted Central Asian sand plover that winters in India: Temminck's specimen was Russian and Gould knew it from Indian collections. The adult's chestnut breast blends into the white throat with no black border, as in the Tibetan group. The small white forehead spots are the one point against.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxiv; the plate

reason: Tundra or Taiga Bean Goose? Bill shape decides. The figure's bill is short, deep and mostly black with a narrow pink band behind the nail, and Gould stresses the 'diminutive bill', which says Tundra (rossicus). A Taiga bird has a long slender bill with more orange. The pink band and pinkish-orange legs also need a Pink-footed Goose ruled out; it was not separated in Britain until 1839.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. vi; the plate

reason: The figure is a Neotropic Cormorant in breeding dress: an orange-yellow gular pouch edged with a thin white line, white filoplumes on the head and neck, and a long tail. Gould's text adds lanceolate scapulars and Temminck's view that Brazilian birds are the same. Temminck lent the specimen. Ogilvie-Grant (Cat. Birds BM xxvi) puts the plate in P. vigua. Linnaeus's graculus is the Shag.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxvi; the plate

reason: Temminck's melanura was killed in Iceland and, Gould says, is a Solan Gannet in every respect but its black tail: a near-adult or aberrant Northern Gannet, not the Cape Gannet. Ogilvie-Grant puts the plate in Sula bassana. The figure's gular stripe is short. The folded wing hides the secondaries, which are all black in a Cape Gannet.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxvi; the plate

reason: Which small black-and-white shearwater? The figure is small and grey-brown above, with white around the eye and white underparts. That fits Barolo Shearwater, the E Atlantic bird nearest Gould's 'Mediterranean and African' range. Salvin cites the plate under P. obscurus, which included Audubon's (now Sargasso). The undertail-covert colour decides: white in Barolo, dark in Sargasso.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxv; the plate

reason: The upper figure is one of Strickland's Tees birds, smaller than Temminck's Cory's: a dark brown cap, white underparts, a dark (not yellow) bill and a pale uppertail patch. That is the Great Shearwater, and Dresser cites the figure under Puffinus major. Gould's description of yellow bill and ash-grey head is Temminck's Cory's.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. viii; the plate

reason: The lower, all-sooty figure is Strickland's Puffinus fuliginosus from the Tees mouth, which Gould took for the young: a Sooty Shearwater. Dresser and Salvin cite this figure under P. griseus.
sources: General List (vol. I); engraved caption; Gould's text; Dresser, B. Eur. viii; Sharpe, Cat. Birds BM xxv; the plate
